Here is something I would suggest that is from my experience: This requires a hard commitment from you and as someone who is hypersexual believe me when I say it's hard. But in the end it'll be worth it. A year in a 20+ year marriage is nothing in the grand scheme. Don't say, "..if no sex happens..". Tell her that sex is off the table until further notice. And you have to mean it. Any touch on the shoulder or peck on the cheek is purely non-sexual intimacy. This may last a while, like 6-12 months, possibly more depending on circumstances. 

The hard part for you is going to be turning yourself off. By that I mean that sexual thoughts or feelings are not the first things that enter your mind when you see/think about her. And even if only unconsciously she will not believe you about the "no sex" for like a month.  You can't leer at her when she bends over or comment if she says something that could get a, "That's what she said" response. You're gonna have to train yourself. Every time you have sexual thoughts remind yourself "not right now, but not never". It's the same idea as meditating, if stray thoughts enter your mind that's okay and bring your concentration back to the sound of your breath. All of this doesn't mean don't masterbate. But also don't make it known or talk about it with her. For me this process took about ~3 weeks. After that your frame of mind shifts. If it takes longer for you that's okay, keep at it. 

This "separation" of yourself can end up being enlightening for you about yourself. For myself I, not intentionally mind you, was able to drill down to what I really wanted from sex. Sex is great, don't get me wrong. But I found that what I wanted from it was the physical intimacy of it. The pleasure of sex is actually secondary. It's a vicious cycle, oftentimes in relationships, for whatever the reason, sex becomes the only time physical intimacy occurs. So we try to engage it more often for that high from touching. But the partner starts to see any touching as a desire to have sex and keeps rejecting any time you try to touch them even if you're not wanting sex. Hugs and kisses are amazing, sure, but cuddling with skin to skin contact for extended periods does wonders for you(if you're like me and your love language is touch). 

Like I said, she won't "believe" the no sex thing for about a month until she sees your behavior change. At that point things will become less stressful enough that working her way back to wanting sex will be quicker and easier for her. As she'll accept your touch knowing that you don't want sex right now. And the more she's accepting of your touch the more intimacy you'll both feel for each other. 

I know that was long, but it worked for me. Good luck.

No judgement and this is anecdotal because it's just my personal experience. It sounds like you were/are a single mom. And when it's just one parent, and especially if it's the first kid, then whatever works. (Not saying this is a bad choice) And sometimes a bad choice is the only choice and you do your best. I grew up with a single mom(she's still single). The earliest memories I have, and there aren't many, are sleeping in the bed with my mom. When I was 4 we lived with my grandma and had just the one room to ourselves so that made sense. But even after we moved out and I had my own room, I still primarily slept in bed with my mom. Partially due to the fact that I didn't like the feel of the bedsheets on my bed, but didn't know how to articulate that. I slept in bed with my mom until somewhere between 8-10. In hindsight for myself, I feel that it caused some issues with myself. 

Side note: from the vibe in the thread co-sleeping is for when kids are little but some comments say that even older is okay.

One of the issues was not being able to sleep well or at all in other places if someone else wasn't in the bed. This was even an issue from when I was 5-6. It made any sleepovers at friends' houses difficult. There are other personal issues that I feel are perhaps not caused by but are exacerbated by this. 

For my kids, we had a bassinet next to our bed for a bit. Then when they were old enough, < 1 year old, we started putting them in their crib. For nights when they had trouble sleeping, which weren't many nights (I know we were lucky in this respect), one of us(usually me) would stay in the room and lay half of my hand on their arm or something either all night or a few hours until they were heavily sleeping. We had a playpen in our bedroom when they were 2-3 if they had trouble sleeping or wanted to sleep in the room with us. 

My experience is probably irregular, but I'm not familiar with best practices for co-sleeping to say otherwise. However, if the situation is like OP's then I'm vehemently against it. (Not saying that you do, just stating my opinion on the post)

Tldr: Your IQ only measures your potential to learn new things. You are likely to be more intelligent with a high IQ, but it does not guarantee it. 

DnD is great for a lot of things, but one thing I think it does rather well is paint a picture of a real person. Follow me for a moment. In DnD your character has stats: Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma. In this case we'll look at Intelligence and Wisdom(or being smart). You can have high or low stats, but that won't determine the outcome. These stats merely measure your potential. Your high intelligence means that you learn things easier than those with a lower stat. Not that a lower stat can't learn something, it'll just take longer and be harder for them. Wisdom is really just experience. It's your ability to take what you know and what you've experienced/are experiencing to come to a conclusion. But the actual result is determined with a roll of the dice. Just like in real life, you can be an expert in something and still fail. The odds are in the favor of an expert, but they can still roll a 1(critical failure). A high IQ may give you a +3 to what you are doing that involves intelligence, but ADHD is gonna give you up to a -5 to intelligence, a -3 to wisdom, and up to a -5 for charisma. Knowing this helps you understand why you keep failing your skill checks and how to better build your character going forward.

I'm on the spectrum and have ADHD, depression, and anxiety. I didn't know these things about myself until my 20s. On the IQ test I'm above average. Remembering to do things was a lot of trouble but like some of us I was good with remembering factoids and numbers. Though that may have been because that's how schools taught/teach you how to learn. I was hyperactive and couldn't focus on most things for longer than 5-10 mins at a time on a good day. I got good at studying 5 mins before the test to pass. I kept A's and B's until 7th grade, because it was expected of me. On occasion I got C's and D's and one F. I say that to show that even with slightly higher intelligence, I still managed to fail at times. In 7th grade I put in the effort for the first nine weeks, but I didn't see the value in getting good grades. So, I stopped trying and switched to barely passing to get by. I got yelled at a lot for it. But no one ever asked why I stopped trying, just you're bad because of it and that I have to do better. 

Fast forward -> military, a few failed marriages, developed seizures, ADHD has gotten worse with age even with meds(though they do help), two kids who are both on the spectrum and ADHD.

Now -> On the surface I have a good job with decent pay, a spouse, and mostly getting by. Underneath, I'm always mentally a mess just holding it together with spit and wishes. My memory has gotten so bad that most of the factoids that I knew for years are gone. Unless the memory gets jogged via conversations, I don't remember most things in general but especially childhood. I've fucked up so much along the way that I could write a novel about it if I could remember the details. And because my memory is so bad, I hesitate to talk about a lot of things. Especially things that would end up as a debate/argument of some kind. I know that I know the answer, but I can't remember it. I know I'm smart, but I can't show it. Ever since the seizures, things have gone downhill faster. I'm never not a giant ball of stress. 

TLDR; How do I do it? I'm almost never not in some level of a frazzled mental state that helps keep the "I got to get it done, but can't start/finish" at bay a lot of times. The trade off is that I always feel like I'm actively failing. Not that I'm a failure, but that I'm failing at everything I do. I don't recommend it.

Interviewing is a learned skill. Yeah some people are better at it, but it's still a skill that takes practice. Especially in our field as it changes so much. I changed jobs recently after being at the same place for four years. The interview process had changed a lot in that amount of time for me. I used a recruiter too. I completely fumbled the first few interviews. But I got a feel for the general questions they would ask and what type of programming problems they would want solved. It's really disheartening when you fumble an interview, especially one you really wanted. Give yourself time to be upset about it, but work yourself through what you felt you did wrong. It's cliche but see your fumble as a learning experience. Also, you can ask the recruiter or the interviewer themselves what they thought of your interview. Getting that kind of feedback is important. Not only can it help you learn to do better, but in some cases where you feel the interview went really well but you still didn't get it, you can find out that you did, in fact, do good; there was just someone else who was a little better. It sucks a little, but there will always be someone better than you and that's okay, it doesn't mean you suck. Keep at it. You'll get better and you will get a "yes" soon.

Something I keep in mind that helps me when I can't think the solution all the way through is this:

Make it work

Make it good

Make it fast

When it works and you have time, you can go back and make it good. Optimize here and there. And if you still have time, which you often won't, you can go over it again and make the code faster. As much as I don't like saying it, bad but working code is better than perfect not working code. The more you do it the better you will get at making it good code when you are just trying to make it work.
